content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued guidelines on the intake of saturated and trans-fatty acids for both adults and children. These guidelines are based on extensive research and aim to reduce the risk of cardiovascular diseases and other health complications associated with unhealthy fat consumption. Studies such as the Special Turku Coronary Risk Factor Intervention Project (STRIP) have demonstrated the long-term benefits of dietary counseling initiated in infancy, showing significant improvements in cardiometabolic risk factors even six years after the intervention. Research published in The Lancet and other journals highlights the growing epidemic of coronary heart disease, particularly in lowand middle-income countries, and underscores the importance of public awareness and education about cardiovascular risk factors. Efforts to address these issues include policy interventions, such as the Danish saturated fat tax, which has been shown to influence food and nutrient intake positively. Similarly, global initiatives to eliminate industrial trans fats, as outlined in WHO's 2022 report, have demonstrated significant health benefits and cost-effectiveness in various countries, including Australia and Canada. Socioeconomic factors also play a critical role in cardiovascular outcomes, as highlighted by studies in Circulation and The Lancet Global Health. These studies emphasize the need for targeted interventions in low-income and lower-middle-income countries to address behavioral risk factors for non-communicable diseases. Dietary recommendations from WHO include reducing saturated fat intake and replacing it with unsaturated fats, increasing the consumption of fruits, vegetables, legumes, and whole grains, and limiting the intake of added sugars and sodium. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses have consistently shown that higher consumption of plant-based foods and nuts is associated with a reduced risk of cardiovascular disease, cancer, and all-cause mortality. The development of these guidelines involved contributions from a diverse group of experts in nutrition, public health, and epidemiology. The guidelines aim to provide evidence-based strategies to promote healthy diets and reduce the global burden of diet-related diseases.
